newsitem.title: GERMANY: German anti-smokers cheered by U.S. tobacco deal.
newsitem.headline: German anti-smokers cheered by U.S. tobacco deal.

text.p: Anti-smoking crusaders said on Monday last week's landmark U.S. settlement with the tobacco industry might boost a flagging campaign for public smoking limits, but saw no chance of such a legal bargain in Germany.

Parliamentary leaders, trying in vain to push through legislation to protect non-smokers, said they expected the $365 billion settlement in the United States to help revive the efforts that powerful tobacco lobbies have been thwarting.
"(It) will give an important push to pass through a bill to protect non-smokers," said Roland Sauer, a member of parliament from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrat (CDU) party.

"Studies have found that second-hand smoke kills 400 people each year in Germany," Sauer added. "We have to protect the health of non-smokers. The subsidiaries of U.S. tobacco firms in Germany would be well-advised to heed the message and drop their massive resistance to the measure."

But Sauer and leaders from the cigarette industry said German product liability laws were fundamentally different from those in the U.S. and there was no real chance companies here could be held accountable for the effects of tobacco.
A cross-party alliance including members of Kohl's centre-right coalition along with the opposition Social Democrats and Greens introduced a bill last year that would have curtailed smokers' rights.
But the measure ran into stiff opposition from tobacco lobbies and has since been stalled in parliamentary committees.
Unlike in the U.S, there are hardly any restrictions on smoking in Germany, where non-smoking sections in restaurants are rare and many workers smoke in offices next to non-smoking colleagues.

Store clerks and theatre ticket sales staff sometimes blow smoke at customers when giving change. It is not uncommon to walk into a smoke-filled elevator and smokers regularly light up whenever a line forms.
Germany is Europe's wealthiest nation and smokers spend 33.4 billion marks ($19.3 billion) on cigarettes each year. Taxes account for three quarters of the average package price of five marks.

Klaus Lennartz, an SPD member of parliament, said the Bundestag should hold public hearings about the dangers of tobacco and force tobacco companies to contribute money to funds that would help cover the costs of smoking-related illnesses.

"If it is possible in the cradle of capitalism, it should be possible in Germany," Lennartz said. "We should have public hearings in parliament in front of as large an audience as possible about the dangers of tobacco consumption."
Lennartz added that if tobacco companies in Germany refuse to voluntarily contribute to such funds then lawmakers "will have to get involved."
Klaus Kirschner, health spokesman for the SPD, said that such a fund should be paid for by smokers through taxation.
